     5	Each bold rule states the rule of this tree. A sentence that names a POSITIONS entry (P-N) states a decision of the curator. Build on a sentence without one, but do not cite it as a decision. Question a rule only on new evidence (`SKILL.md`, "When to explore"). Most rules follow the team's later type papers (`Papers/`) over the specification's early text (P-26; `exploring.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. Where a rule changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`).
     6	
     7	A sentence that cites a ledger row states a behaviour that is not settled: a known departure from a rule, or a case that the rules do not decide yet. Either can change, so do not assert it in a plain test. Where the rules decide the case, an `XXX` test asserts their answer (`tests-writing.md`). A sentence that opens "Until the switch-over" states a limit of the compiler's library. The limit ends when the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, so do not fix it in the compiler's prelude (`compiler.md`). If a change is not here, search FACTS and POSITIONS (`records.md`) before you call a disagreement a conflict. An old note, a team test and your training can be right about the team's walk and wrong here: the number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, and walk converts arguments.
     8	
     9	## Dispatch and overloading
    10	
    11	**Overloads may differ in their static parameters (P-45).** An example is `ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T` beside `ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T`. The Working Draft forbids such pairs. A declaration's declared domain is the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept at some instance within its bounds: every `Shape` for the first `ident`. The checker applies the overloading rules of `SKILL.md` to declared domains. The more specific declaration's return type must be a subtype of the other's at every instance that the argument types allow, not at one only.
    12	
    13	**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value has at most one instance of a given generic type. So where both declarations name the same generic type at a position, a value of both domains makes the two static arguments equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair whose exclusion needs a static parameter that the equalities leave free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.
    14	
    15	**Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations.** It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".
    16	
    17	**Walk's load check is not the verdict of these rules.** It refuses some valid pairs and loads some invalid ones, and the checker differs from it on others. Before you change code to pass walk's check, or take its acceptance as proof, find the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks": a case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk. For example, walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object at each call, not at load (row 780).
    18	
    19	**Two functional methods with equivalent parameter types are duplicates, wherever `self` stands.** So the checker refuses `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` in a trait `S`. Abstract declarations count:
    20	
    21	- both paths refuse an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one trait;
    22	- both paths refuse an object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another, unless the object declares the method itself (P-149). The Scala language accepts it.
    23	
    24	The Meet Rule asks for a declaration that covers the meet of two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest (`SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language"). An abstract functional method is an overload for this rule too. So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`. Likewise, a program's trait that declares its own functional `+` overlaps the library's `+` between an array and a number, because a type can extend both the trait and `Number`, which has no `comprises` clause (P-160). Declare the trait `excludes { Number }`, or, for a number type below `Number`, `excludes { HasRank }`, the trait that arrays extend. Or declare the `+` in an object, not in a trait: an object excludes every trait that it does not extend, because no other type can extend it. Otherwise walk refuses the program at load: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker refuses such a pair in one component, but accepts it against the library's `+` (row 918). Give a trait with its own functional `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` the same fix: the library declares these in the same form.
    25	
    26	## Traits and objects
    27	
    28	**The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97).** It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk does not apply the rule: it runs such a type, and refuses overloads on two instantiations, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, because it does not read them as excluding (row 416). The specification marks the Working Draft's examples that break the rule "Not allowed": do not copy them.
    29	
    30	**A `comprises` clause speaks of values (P-60).** Every value of the trait that declares it is a value of a listed type. So a generic trait need not be listed if every type below it is below a listed type, as `Integral[\I\]` below `AnyIntegral`. A Java `permits` list names each direct subtype; this clause need not. So where the Meet Rule asks for a declaration at the meet of two overloads, several declarations that together cover the meet serve. At load, walk checks extenders only against the clauses of the program's main component (row 551).
    31	
    32	**`override` widens.** An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than its own. To replace an inherited declaration at its own parameter types, declare it again without `override`. The checker refuses such a redeclaration where an object reaches the method of a generic self-typed trait along two paths (row 1037). An `override` in a trait also overrides in every type below it. The checker checks that an overriding return type is a subtype. Walk refuses at load an `override` that, by this rule, overrides nothing, so a Java-style `override` in the library stops every program. Two departures: the checker accepts such an `override` (row 653), and the code generator refuses every `override` modifier, so a program that writes one does not compile (row 650).
    33	
    34	**An object defines an inherited abstract method by bodies that together cover its parameter types (P-147).** It needs one body at those types, or several narrower bodies that cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk refuses at load an object without static parameters that leaves one uncovered. Walk skips this check for a generic object (row 665). Walk and the checker stop the search for a cover at the same limits, which `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", gives. The checker refuses a cover by several bodies where the abstract or a covering method has static parameters (row 725).
    35	
    36	**In a self-typed trait the checker types `self` as the trait met with the implementing type.** A trait `T` is self-typed if both conditions hold:
    37	
    38	- `T` has no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`;
    39	- `T` has a parameter `X` bounded by `T` itself, as `trait T[\X extends T[\X\]\]` (P-146), or by a self-typed trait `U[\X\]` that `T` extends, as `trait T[\X extends U[\X\]\] extends U[\X\]`.
    40	
    41	In `T`'s bodies, `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X`. So `floor(self): I = self` in `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` is valid without a cast. The checker refuses a type that extends `T[\A\]` and is not an `A`. A compiled body of `T` that returns `self` at `X` runs. Three shapes fail when the class loads:
    42	
    43	- a function expression or a local function that returns `self` at `X` fails the JVM's verification (row 1050);
    44	- a conditional with `self` in one arm and another value in the other fails the JVM's verification (row 1051). `StandardTotalOrder`'s `MIN` and `MAX` in the interpreter's library have this shape. So declare your own `MIN` and `MAX` in a type that extends `StandardTotalOrder` and must run compiled, as the integer types do;
    45	- a body that `T` gives one of its methods, which calls a method on a value of type `X`, gives a `ClassCircularityError` where the object lists `T` first in its `extends` clause (row 1052).
    46	
    47	For the first two shapes, bind `self` to a variable of type `X` first, as `s: X = self`, and use `s`. For the third shape, declare the method in `T` without a body, and give the body in the object. Declaring it again in the object while `T` keeps its body still fails.
    48	
    49	When the checker applies the overloading rules to a method of `T`, `self` has the type `T[\X\]`, except in its test of whether two domains exclude each other. There `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X` (P-157). With this reading and the bounds that the test reads ("Dispatch and overloading"), the library's generic `+` and `-` between an array and a number are valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own. Walk reads `self` in the same way, so it loads such a pair in the library and in a program's own component. In two cases walk does not read `self` so, and its load check refuses the valid pair:
    50	
    51	- `T` is self-typed only through another self-typed trait that it extends;
    52	- `T`'s method has static parameters of its own.
    53	
    54	**An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (P-156).** An indexed type is a type whose values take a subscript, as `a[i]`: an array, for example. Its index parameter is the static parameter that gives the type of `i`. In the library, and in your own generic over such a type, write `I extends Index`. Walk runs the code without the bound. The checker refuses it when it checks against the interpreter's library, as the count stage does (`compiler.md`). Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `Index`, so a program that names it does not compile: write the bound only in code that runs under walk or is checked against the interpreter's library.
    55	
    56	Of the integer types, only `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes `Index`. A numeral at a parameter of type `Index` takes its default, a `ZZ32`, so `f(3)` is valid for `f(x: Index)`. The Working Draft lets no trait type hold a tuple, but here a tuple whose element types are all `Index` types is an `Index`. So `m[i, j]` passes the pair `(i, j)` as one index. `Index` extends only `Any`, so such a tuple is still no `Object`. The empty tuple `()` is no `Index`. A function over `Index` and one over a tuple of `Index` types do not exclude each other. Two departures:
    57	
    58	- the checker refuses a tuple expression at a parameter of type `Index`, but takes one at a parameter of type `I`, where `I extends Index` (row 805);
    59	- walk loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it (row 806).
    60

    65	- values of different types are never equivalent;
    66	- a value object is equivalent field by field, a tuple element by element, an integer, a character or a boolean by its value, and a float by its bits;

At a number type, the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, and `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`. A numeral outside the type's range, or that rounds to an infinity there, is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the place runs. Walk's message depends on the place: a top-level binding gives 'Type mismatch binding', a parameter 'got arg'. To get an infinity, overflow run-time arithmetic: for `t: RR64 = 10.0^308`, `t TIMES 10.0` is `Infinity` under walk. `x.isInfinite` tests for one. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares neither `TIMES` nor `isInfinite`.
   102	
   103	Elsewhere the numeral takes its default: `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. Elsewhere includes an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, `Index` and an unbounded type parameter. So `n = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64`, and `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\RR64\]`. The default stays the value's type: for `x = 0.1`, `q: QQ = x` is refused. A type parameter that numerals alone fix takes the narrowest default that holds them all. A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value, other than a numeral type's number, is a `ZZ32`, so `u: NN32 = n` is refused (P-173, P-40). Such a parameter of 2^31 or more is a `ZZ64` under walk, and raises an error on the compiled path (row 962).
   104	
   105	Write a numeral type only as the parameter type of a coercion or an operator. The checker refuses it as the type of a variable, a field or a return (P-174). A program's own number type takes a numeral through a coercion generic over its numbers, which its body declares, as `value object Byte(b: ZZ32)` declares `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 } = Byte(v.asZZ32)`. With a radix point, write `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\])`. The coercion's body reads `n`, `r` and `v` as `ZZ` values without a bound, since a numeral's digits fit no fixed width (P-173, P-40). The `where` clause bounds the numerals that the type takes. The checker refuses statically a numeral that breaks it, as `300` here: 'The numeral 300 does not meet the where clause of the coercion to Byte.' Walk refuses it when the binding runs. A negative constant, as `-3`, reaches the type as the type's prefix `-` on the coercion's result for `3`, so a type without `-` refuses it. The coercion gives one value for each place where the numeral is written, and each run of that place reuses it (P-176). Without such a coercion, the type refuses a numeral. The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or a `Matrix` only at the eight number types; at a program's own number type they give a plain array. `interpreter.md` and `compiler.md` give the other departures from these rules.
   106	
   107	**An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker, on both paths (P-173).** The fold covers the arithmetic operators, `^` up to the exponent 4096, `MIN`, `MAX`, the comparisons, and `DIV`, `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD`, `LCM`, `CHOOSE` and `MINMAX` over integers. It leaves alone the wrapping, saturating and bitwise operators, the shifts, a division by zero, an integer base at a negative exponent, and a result that can be `-0.0`. A folded comparison is a boolean. Any other result is one exact constant, which converts as a numeral does at one of the eight number types, or takes its default. A quotient that is not whole stays `n / d` in lowest terms and defaults to a `QQ`. So `2147483647 + 1` is the `ZZ64` 2147483648, not an `IntegerOverflow`, `(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3)` is `true`, and under walk `lr = 1/1000` is a `QQ`. Except for a negated numeral, as `-3` above, a program's own type takes the constant only through a coercion from its default type, since coercions do not chain (P-174). So `h: Half = 10/20` needs `coerce(q: QQ)`; a numeral coercion is not enough. `||` of string literals folds into one literal (P-171). A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand: write `m: ZZ32 = 2147483647`, then `m + 1`, or `t: String = "ab"`, then `t || "c"`.
   108	
   109	**Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts a value other than a numeral at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). The rule converts at a declared return type too, but walk does not (row 387). Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". If one of them takes the call's numerals at their default, it runs instead: `1.0 s` for `s: ZZ32` is `RR64`'s product, not `QQ`'s.
   110	
   111	**A numeral can run a more specific declaration than the one that fits its default type (P-46).** On both paths, a call with a numeral runs the declaration that fits the numeral's default type, unless the numeral's coercion reaches another declaration whose declared parameter types are strict subtypes of the first one's. Then the other runs. So `k(5)` runs `k(x: NN32)` beside `k(x: Any)`, but `f(1.5)` runs `f(x: RR64)` beside `f(x: RR32)`. Two departures:
   112	
   113	- under walk, a numeral in a call whose other argument is a variable declared `Any` converts by that value's run-time type, as `a = 0` for `a: Any` (row 1016);
   114	- on both paths, `g(5)` runs `g[\T\](x: T)` beside `g(x: NN32)`, where the rule gives `g(x: NN32)` (row 1017).
   115	
   116	**An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161).** To convert a value, write a getter, as `x.asZZ32`: `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` or `asZZ`. It keeps the value or raises `IntegerOverflow`. The low-bits functions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's `(int)` does. On the fixed-width types, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, `narrow` and `widen` give the 32-bit and the 64-bit type of the same sign, `signed` and `unsigned` the signed and the unsigned type of the same width, and `big` a `ZZ`. So `narrow` of a `ZZ64` outside `ZZ32`'s range wraps silently. In the interpreter's library, each fixed-width type has all five functions, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`. `ZZ` has only `big`, so for a `ZZ` value `z`, `narrow(z)` finds no declaration: write `z.asZZ32`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has only these getters: `asZZ` on each fixed-width type, `asZZ32` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, `asNN32` on `NN32`, and `asNN64` on `NN64`. It has no `big`, and of the low-bits functions only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349).
   117	
   118	**`Number` declares nothing (P-165).** Each of the eight number types declares its own functional method `asFloat(self): RR64`. So generic code over `T extends Number` can call on a `T` no method or operator that the number types declare, `asFloat` among them. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares `=` for each such pair, so a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` of equal value are `=`. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error, as for a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. A numeral reaches a number type's own `=` by its coercion (P-46). So on both paths `u = 0` and `0 = u` are `true` and `u =/= 0` is `false` for a zero `u: NN32`, and `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`. To compare values across types at known types, write `asFloat(x) = y`. In generic code over `T extends Number`, declare your function once for each number type instead.
   119	
   120	**An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included.
   121	**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. No coercion carries a `ZZ64` into `RR64`, so convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.
   122	
   123	## Reductions and comprehensions
   124	
   125	A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.
   126	
   127	**Where a reduction's bound names its parameter, as for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, the two paths fix an unwritten static argument from different places.** The argument is written as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Without it, the checker takes the reduction's expected type, and the body's type only where there is no expected type or it does not fit the reduction's bound. So `x: RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)` sums `ZZ32` elements in `RR64`, not in the body's type. A reduction whose bound does not name its parameter takes its bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types; if it is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1".
   128	
   129	At a method's return type, a field, a top-level variable and an assignment, the checker reads the declared type, so the two paths sum in different types (row 1008): `meth(): RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#4] huge(j)` raises `IntegerOverflow` under walk only. Write the argument there in a program for both paths. A call's argument has no expected type where the call is accepted without one. So as a call's argument, a reduction sums in its body's type on both paths. Write both arguments of `BIG MIN_MAX`, the element types of its pairs, as `BIG MIN_MAX[\ZZ32, ZZ32\][j <- 0#3] pr(j)`: the checker infers only a single static parameter (row 1007). Departures under walk:
   130	
   131	- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
   132	- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (row 717);
   133	- a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).
   134	
   135	**A reduction without an identity lifts its elements to `Maybe[\R\]` inside the reduction.** `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and the string reduction `BIG //` extend `AssociativeReduction[\R\]`, whose `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`. `BIG MAX` over a generator still answers `R`. Walk refuses at load a reduction without static parameters that declares `simpleJoin` at `Any` or untyped. A generic one stops at its first join. The team's tests declare `simpleJoin` so: do not copy them.
   136	
   137	## Implementation limits
   138	
   139	**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). Besides a `Boolean`, walk takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition.
   140	
   141	**Write every parameter type.** The compiled checker refuses a parameter without a type, "Missing parameter type for", unless the exported api's declaration gives the type. Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types. With none or several, the checker types the body.

# Working in the Fortress revival repository

The team at Sun Labs built the Fortress language from 2003 to 2012 and left it unfinished. This repository finishes their design from what they left: the code, the specification and the papers. The goal is the model program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**brief**
: Instructions that you were launched with. It gives your mission.

**original tree**
: What the team left in this repository: the code, the specification, the papers and their git history. On disk, it is everything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`.

**record**
: Project's memory: the files under `explorations/` that hold what the project has established, decided and measured (below).

**walk**
: Interpreter, and the default command of `bin/fortress`: `bin/fortress P.fss` is the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`.

**compiled path**
: Other way to run a program: `bin/fortress compile P.fss` writes JVM bytecode, and `bin/fortress run P` runs it.

**model program**
: microGPT, the program by which the revival is measured. It has two programs: the flat program, which the record calls C4 (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), and the APL program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`). Each has a quick check beside it, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`. A model line is a source line of either program.

**one library**
: Interpreter's library, which both paths use after the switch-over (below).

**component**
: Unit of Fortress code, in a `.fss` file of its own name. A component implements the apis that it exports, and uses the apis that it imports.

**api**
: Interface, in a `.fsi` file of its own name.

**area**
: One part of the system: the interpreter, the compiled path (the checker, the code generator and the runtime), the library, or the specification.

**base**
: Commit that your work starts from.

**gate**
: Full check of a tree before it lands, when a brief asks for it. To land a tree is to commit it to `main` and push `main`.

**harness**
: Suites' own test runner. Each test is a whole Fortress program, not a JUnit test of a Java class. The harness runs the program and checks the result, as LLVM's lit does for Swift's test suite. `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` run it on the files that you name.

**building**
: Normal mode of work where you carry out the mission of your brief. You take the facts and the curator's decisions in the record as given.

**exploring**
: Mode of work for a question that the record does not settle. You gather evidence, first in the record and then in the original tree. You add what you found to the record, and then go back to building.

You work with three things: your brief, the record and the original tree. Building happens in one area at a time, so this skill has one part for each area.

## How a program runs

Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you edit a phase that both paths run, or a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives"), run your test on both paths. `references/compiler.md`, "Natives", says how to test such a class on the compiled path. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.

### The phases

Each path runs these phases on each component, in this order (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java`):

1. Parse the source into a syntax tree. This tree is the only form of the program, from the parser to the bytecode.
2. Bind each name to its declaration.
3. Expand the DSL grammars that the component imports (`references/build-and-caches.md`).
4. Fold each expression of numerals alone into one exact value: a numeral, a quotient of two numerals or a boolean (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers").
5. Check the static types. Walk's phase list holds this phase, but walk switches it off.
6. Desugar: comprehensions and big operators become calls, and getters and setters become methods.
7. Mark each call of an overloaded name.

Walk then interprets the tree. The tree has no static types, so walk finds a type error only at run time, as a failed dispatch. A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed, unlike in Java or Scala.

`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.

Each path has its own library today. At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The compiled checker already finds no error in the interpreter's library. For the `FortressLibrary` component, the count stage shows this as a total of 0 (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over waits for walk's natives: each function that the interpreter's library binds with `builtinPrimitive` (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives") must first have a binding that the compiled path runs.

### The compiled runtime

`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:

- the component's functions, objects and traits;
- its closures;
- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.

A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.

The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).

HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.

### The caches

A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.

- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"`.
- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.

In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).

`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.

### Parallelism and mutable state

Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.

`x = e` declares an immutable variable. `var x: T = e` and `x: T := e` declare a mutable one, and `x := e` assigns to it (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`). These are Scala's `val` and `var`, or Swift's `let` and `var`. A field is immutable unless it is declared with `var`. A value object is a tuple, `()`, or an object whose declaration, or a trait that it extends, has the `value` modifier, as the library's numbers, characters and booleans do. It has only immutable fields and value semantics, like a Swift `struct`. Nothing refuses a `var` field in a value object, so give it none. Any other object, except a function, is a reference object, like an instance of a Swift class. Each construction makes a new reference object, distinct from all others (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:24-33`).

Parallel code stays free of races in these ways:

- Most data is immutable.
- A big operator, such as `SUM` or `BIG MAX`, combines the results of its tasks, as OpenMP's reduction clause does. No task writes a shared accumulator. The specification's reduction variables are not built.
- A write to shared state goes inside an `atomic` block. This is software transactional memory, like Haskell's `atomically` (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`). The programmer writes `atomic`; the compiler adds none.
- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").

So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.

Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes, an object's `var` field among them. From the switch-over, it also tracks each array element that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).

An `exit` out of an `atomic` block loses the block's writes, on both paths (ledger row 1039). Set a flag in the block, and exit after the block.

## Fortress as a language

Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.

- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's: the Return Type Rule. Walk checks part of this at load.
- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (a `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`, but a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's numbers: `references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion does not change which declaration runs when one already fits. A numeral is the one exception: it can run a more specific declaration that its coercion reaches. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`, but an expression of numerals alone folds exactly (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"). The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

## The record

The record's main files:

- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions.
- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the original tree. Each fact names its test and points to the report that holds its detail.
- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line for each note under `explorations/`.
- `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, the gap ledger: the known gaps, one row each.

Read a slice of the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`. `references/records.md` lists its queries.

## When to explore

Switch from building to exploring when you meet one of these:

- A gap: something missing or broken that the record does not know.
- A conflict: two of the team's sources disagree, and no decision of the curator says which one is correct. The team's sources are the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations.
- New evidence against a decision of the curator. Evidence is new only if the decision did not use it. Your own view of the evidence that it used is not new evidence.

When you switch, load `references/exploring.md`. It says which choices are yours and which go to the curator.

## Rules for every task

- Carry out the curator's decisions as the record states them.
- If the record does not settle a question that your work meets, switch to exploring.
- Cite a source for each claim that you write: your brief, an entry of the record, or a primary source (the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output).
- Reproduce a behaviour before you explain it: run a command that shows it, unless your brief cites the command's output.
- When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause.

## How a defect is recorded

Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:

1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. If walk crashes on the program, still write the `XXX` test, unlike under 3: the harness counts the crash as the expected failure. A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.
3. It is deferred, and the specification is silent or a conflict leaves it open (`exploring.md`): a test that asserts today's behaviour, and a row in the gap ledger (`records.md`). If no program can observe the defect, or no gated test can pass while it shows, as when walk crashes on the program, write the ledger row only. Its reproducer, the row's cell that names the test, is `none`, and its notes give the command and its output.

If your brief does not let you edit the original tree, say in your report which of the three the defect needs, and write a ledger row for it, whichever it needs. The change that next works there writes the test.

## The order: the test, its failure, the fix, the pass

1. Write the test, with a plain name. Write the essence of the defect as a clean, minimal program, not the shape in which a probe met it.
2. See the test fail through the harness (`harness-one.sh` or `junit.sh`, `tests-running.md`) on the base's code. Do this in a run that ends before you first build or compile your edit. Under walk, do it before you edit a library source that the test reads. If your tree already holds the fix, run the test through the harness on the old code, as `worktrees.md`, "Running the old code", says.
3. Make the fix. See the test pass in your last run after your last change of code.

The test needs no commit of its own. A test that comes with no fix has no failing run: see it pass through the harness.

In your report, quote two to five lines of the failing run, if there is one, and the passing line, each with its command. In an edit of the original tree, put every check into a gated test, never into a one-off script. A task that only measures may use its own script. Assert a value with `assert` in an interpreter test. In a compiled test, assert it with `assert` (above), or print it and check it with a `run_out_equals` key.

An edit of prose in `Specification/` or `Documentation/` has no test. Check it as `specification.md`, "Changing the text: the revision form", says.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:71
- P-160 **The one library's `Number` opens: its `comprises` clause goes, so that a program may declare its own number type below `Number`.** The team's compiler prelude, the specification and the team's test `tests/extendNumber.fss` give `Number` no such clause. It went in two steps. First, walk reads the library's scalar `+` and `-` between an array and a number beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own operator, as the compiled checker does (P-152, the exclusion of two generic declarations; row 804, its walk half). Then the clause was removed from `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi` (F-324); the reflective QuickCheck generator got a way to generate a `Number`, `Number`'s `=` and `asFloat` left the trait (P-165), so that a program's own number type compares by its own `=` or by the library's fallback `=` through `SEQV`, and the tests that leaned on the clause were repaired. The clause stayed until the first step landed (F-318): without it, walk refused the library's array operators at load, and with them most programs. `AnyIntegral`'s clause stays (P-44). Why: the clause does no work for the compiled checker, whose count of errors in the one library and distance to the switch-over are 0 with it and without it; and a vector or matrix of a program's own complex numbers needs it gone, since the library bounds `Vector` and `Matrix` by `Number` and `MultiplicativeRing`.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:107
- P-178 **Each built-in number type is one `value object` under its own name, and walk's native number objects `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` go.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64` and `RR64` are each declared `value object`, as `NN32` and `RR32` already are, in place of a trait with one native object below it, such as `trait ZZ32 comprises { Int }` with `value object Int extends ZZ32`. An object is a leaf, so no type of a program extends a built-in number type; a program's own number type extends `Number` (P-160). Compiled code can then hold a value of such a type as a bare JVM `int`, `long` or `double` (P-17), and both paths take this form before the switch-over: the one library by the merge, and the compiler's prelude by an exception to P-37, as for the numerals, which goes with the prelude. For the number types it replaces the pattern that P-164's reason names, a trait with walk's native object below it. Why: the two names are a duality between the two libraries, which the curator called a problem that the revival makes for itself by keeping it; the second names are walk's internals, which a program is not to see (P-167); and the compiler prelude's open trait lets a program's object extend `ZZ32`, which a bare `int` cannot hold (row 866, such a program compiles and dies when it runs). Detail: `reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md`, "Way D. One object per type: each number trait merged with its one object"; the merge as probed: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/number-object-merge.md`, "What was built".

.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md:89:**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor. Two sizes are equal when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic: `2 3` is `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).
.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md:105:**An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker, on both paths (P-173).** The fold covers the arithmetic operators, `^` up to the exponent 4096, `MIN`, `MAX`, the comparisons, and `DIV`, `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD`, `LCM`, `CHOOSE` and `MINMAX` over integers. It leaves alone the wrapping, saturating and bitwise operators, the shifts, a division by zero, an integer base at a negative exponent, and a result that can be `-0.0`. A folded comparison is a boolean. Any other result is one exact constant, which converts as a numeral does at one of the eight number types, or takes its default. A quotient that is not whole stays `n / d` in lowest terms and defaults to a `QQ`. So `2147483647 + 1` is the `ZZ64` 2147483648, not an `IntegerOverflow`, `(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3)` is `true`, and under walk `lr = 1/1000` is a `QQ`. Except for a negated numeral, as `-3` above, a program's own type takes the constant only through a coercion from its default type, since coercions do not chain (P-174). So `h: Half = 10/20` needs `coerce(q: QQ)`; a numeral coercion is not enough. `||` of string literals folds into one literal (P-171). A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand: write `m: ZZ32 = 2147483647`, then `m + 1`, or `t: String = "ab"`, then `t || "c"`.
.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md:118:**An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).

## Case 36: a `typecase` at walk's old number names, and a program's type below a number type

- **Trap.** A built-in number type is an abstract type with a concrete run-time object below it. A program then names that object in a `typecase`, a type or a test, and a program's own type extends the number type to take its operators, as a Haskell type joins `Num`. Its sources (climb batch 31b's `orientation/admission.md`, F-379's row):
  - the specification's `trait ℤ` (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:229`);
  - the team's library, which declared `trait ZZ32 … comprises { Int, IntLiteral }` with `value object Int extends ZZ32`, and `Float`, `Long`, `UnsignedLong` and `BigNum` in the same way (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fss:642`, and `trait RR64 … comprises { Float, FloatLiteral, RR32, QQ }` at `:422`; `a874948ac:ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:369`, `Int`, and `:54`, `Float`; climb batch 31b's `RECORD.md`, rung O's revival change);
  - the team's `tests/NumberPrintTest.fss`, whose `typecase` had arms at `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` until rung O respelled them (`f6e24650e7`);
  - the skill's area parts, which still name the five as current (`interpreter.md:121`, `:127`, and `:141`, where a program's object that extends `ZZ32` loads; `compiler.md:22`, `:99`; `library.md:39`), as this key's case 29 did until this update;
  - the audit's proposed core line "Numbers are library traits, side by side" (`skills-distillation-audit.md:364`).

  Worker failures. After `IntLiteral` left the one library, `tests/IntegerConversionsWalk.fss`'s `shown` printed '-2147483648 : IntLiteral' for a `ZZ32`, until its arms were removed (row 959's note). Before climb batch 27, 48 lines of revival tests asserted printed `Int` names (case 29's **Trap**). Rung O's skeptic ran the arms `Int`, `Float` and `else` on `3`, `1.5` and `"s"`: the base answered `3 Int; 1.5 Float; s else`, and the landed tree `3 Int; 1.5 Int; s Int`, "the one landed change that turns a right answer into a silent wrong one for a program that still names `Int`" (`reviews/batch-31b-review.md`, section 2, O4). For the extender: on the base, `object Mine extends ZZ32` loaded under walk and failed at its first native method, 'getInt not implemented for FOrdinaryObject' (climb batch 31b's `RECORD.md`, rung O; row 551), and on the compiled path it compiles and dies (row 866). The landing's cold reader, with the core and the area parts but not the orientation, found the skill naming the removed objects as current (`record-landing/cold-read.md:189`, `:196-202`). Neither quiz tests it.
- **Expected.**
  - (a) Both assertions run, and every value takes the first arm: `kind(3)` gives "Int", and `kind(1.5)` gives "Int" too. No library declares `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` or `UnsignedLong` since climb batch 31b (P-178, F-379), and a `typecase` arm at a name that no declaration defines matches every value, with no message (row 959). So the first assertion passes for the wrong reason, and the second fails, 'FAIL: … Int =/= … Float'.
  - (b) Arms at the library's own names: `ZZ32` in place of `Int` and `RR64` in place of `Float`, with `else`; `ZZ64`, `ZZ` and `NN64` stand in place of `Long`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong`. At `kind`'s `Number` parameter the numerals take their defaults, `ZZ32` for `3` and `RR64` for `1.5` (P-173). So the assertions are that `kind(3)` is "ZZ32" and `kind(1.5)` is "RR64". The strings are the test's own: "Int" and "Float" kept as the labels of arms at `ZZ32` and `RR64` are right too. `Meters` goes below `Number`, with its own operators:

        value object Meters(v: ZZ32) extends Number
          opr +(self, other: Meters): Meters = Meters(v + other.v)
        end

    It needs `Number` as a parent to be passed to `kind`. Without it, walk stops at the call, 'Unification error: Closure/Constructor for kind param 1 (x:Number) got arg Meters of type Meters'. `kind(Meters(2))` gives "other", or the label of an arm at `Meters` if the reader adds one. An assertion such as `(Meters(2) + Meters(3)).v` = 5 checks the `+`. A plain `object` in place of `value object` is right too.
  - (c) The planned `object Meters(v: ZZ32) extends ZZ32`: walk refuses the program at load, 'Attempt to extend object type ZZ32'. `ZZ32` is one value object, an object is a leaf, and no type of a program extends a built-in number type (P-178, F-379; `tests/NumberTypeExtendRefusedWalk.fss`). On the compiled path today the checker accepts it, since the compiler's prelude still declares `ZZ32` an open trait (row 1003). The run then dies when the object's class loads, before `run()` prints anything: 'IncompatibleClassChangeError: class …$Meters can not implement com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32, because it is not an interface' (row 866). The reader's `Meters` below `Number` loads and runs under walk, and compiles and runs on the compiled path.
- **Scope.** The arms behave alike on both paths. The team's arms compile and run and send every value to the first arm (row 959 states it on both paths), and the repaired arms compile and run. The extender differs by path today: refused at load under walk, dead at class load when compiled. This holds until the prelude takes P-178's form (decided and not built: review-queue item 577, fork H2) or until the switch-over (row 866, "Ends when"). Other points, none needed for a right answer:
  - A trait of the program's own below `ZZ32` is refused at load under walk too, with the same message (this update's probe; the record has no run of it).
  - A removed name as a type is refused at load: `describe(x: Int)` stops, 'Int is undefined.' (this update's probe; F-303 for `Float`).

- **Wrong.**
  - (a) "Int" and "Float", as the arms read; the program said to be refused at load, or to raise, because of the arms; the first assertion's pass taken as a sign that the arm works.
  - (b) An arm, a type, a test or a message at `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` or `UnsignedLong`, on either path. `Meters` below `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `RR64`, or below a trait of the program's own that extends one. `Meters` with no `Number` parent, passed to `kind`.
  - (c) The planned declaration said to load under walk, to be refused by the compiled checker today, or to compile and run; walk's refusal reported as a defect.
- **Partial.**
  - (a) and (b) right, with no compiled answer in (c), or with the compiled extender said to be refused as it is under walk.
  - (b) right, with no word on why `extends ZZ32` cannot stand.
  - (a) with the second assertion said to fail, but without the value "Int" for `1.5`.

## Case 27: a program's trait with its own `+`, beside the library's `+` between an array and a number

- **Trap.** A trait's own `opr +(self, other: Wide)` overloads nothing of the library, as a method of one's own class does not in Java or Scala. Until climb batch 27 the program loaded: `Number`'s `comprises` clause kept the trait apart from the numbers. A worker failure: the revival's `tests/CoercionOverloadRungC.fss` declared `trait Wide excludes { Narrow, String }` with its own `+`; it loaded on the base, was refused at load once the clause was struck, and was respelled to exclude `Number` (`compile-ladder/rung-number-open/REPORT.md`, "A program that loads today and is refused after"). Neither quiz tests it (climb batch 27's `orientation/admission.md`, P-160's row).
- **Expected.** Under walk the test does not load: walk refuses the program at load, '... fails the Meet Rule: neither is found to be more specific than the other or to exclude it', naming the trait's `+` and the library's `+[\T extends { Number, AdditiveGroup[\T\] }, I extends Index\](x: Array[\T,I\], y: T)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:5061`). `Number` is open (P-160): nothing keeps `Wide` apart from `Number` or from the arrays, so one type can be a `Wide`, an array and a number at once; the two declarations neither exclude each other nor nest, and nothing covers their meet. The compiled checker refuses such a pair where both declarations are in one component, but accepts this program against the one library across the import (row 918): a gap of the checker, not the verdict. The change, for both paths: `trait Wide excludes { String, Number }`, as `CoercionOverloadRungC.fss:6` was respelled, or a clause that excludes the arrays. The program then loads and the assertion passes.
- **Scope.** The library's `-`, `MIN` and `MAX` between an array and a number have the same form (F-119), so a trait with its own `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` meets the same refusal, by reading: only `+` was measured. An object that declares its own `+` and extends neither `Number` nor an array type is a leaf and excludes both (case 12; by reading). Excluding the arrays, by `HasRank`, is by reading: the rung took `Number` (decision 7). Before the switch-over the compiled path reads the compiler's prelude, which has no arrays; no record compiles the program there, and row 918's compiled half waits for the switch-over. None of these points is needed for a right answer.
- **Wrong.** The test said to load and pass; the checker's acceptance taken as the verdict, or as proof that walk is wrong; a change of the library, such as a `comprises` clause put back on `Number` (P-160).
- **Partial.** The walk refusal and the `excludes { Number }` change right, with no word on the checker, or with the checker said to refuse the program across the import; or the operator renamed in place of the clause, with the refusal's cause named.
- **Open.** Walk checks a program's declarations of a library operator name against the library's only on a cold cache (F-269), so a run from warm caches may load the program. F-269 also says that one declaration of the name is not checked, yet the measured program declares one functional `+` and is refused through the harness (`tests/NumberOpenTraitPlusBesideArrayWalk.test`; `rung-number-open/REPORT.md`, "The tests"), and the record does not say whether that run's cache was cold. The record does not reconcile the two, nor measure the program on a warm cache. A reader who says that a run which loads the program proves nothing is right; one who takes such a run as proof that it is valid is wrong.

- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). There are two exceptions, each so that both paths do the same before the switch-over, and each copy goes with the prelude: the numerals, where the prelude carries the design of P-174 and P-176; and the built-in number types, where it takes the form of P-178. The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""skills-lint.py [FILE...]: find the coordinator's agenda in the project skills.

The patterns and their scopes are the "Lint pattern list" of
explorations/reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md:

  fortress-repo and cloud-container, SKILL.md and parts: every set but sources;
  coordinator, SKILL.md and parts: handles (coordinator form), status, stale;
  every references/sources.md: the sources set only.

A file's skill is the folder after "skills/" in its path, so a copy made with
`git show REV:.claude/skills/...` into a folder of the same layout is linted
as the file it copies. A skill not named above takes every set.

With no FILE, every file under the repository's .claude/skills/. Prints
`path:line: set: text` for each hit, the text clipped around the match, and
exits 1 if there is any. Patterns are case-insensitive unless they say (?-i:...).
ALLOW lists hits read and passed, by file, set and a substring of the line.
"""
import os, re, sys

HANDLES = [
    r"\bQ\d+(\.\d+)?\b",
    r"\bitems? (1\d|[2-9]\d|\d{3})[a-z]?\b",
    r"\b(climb )?batch(es)? \d+('s)?\b",
    r"\brung (?!-)[A-Z]\b|\brung's\b",
    r"\b(review|gather|coldread|delta-unfolded|review-routed|judge-review)\.\d+\b",
]
HANDLES_COORDINATOR = HANDLES[:3] + [r"\brung (?!-)[A-Z]\b"]
STATUS = [
    r"\b(pending|unanswered|not (yet )?answered|has not answered|awaiting|still open|leaves the question|to be applied)\b",
    r"\bdoes not yet say\b|\b(is|are) not yet (decided|known|answered)\b",
    r"\bthe default of (Q\d|item \d|way)|\bat (its|the) default\b|\bway \d+[a-z]?\b",
]
PROVENANCE = [
    r"\bcurator('s)? (decided|kept|chose|ruled|answered)\b",
    r"\bthe curator (gives|weighs|keeps)\b",
    r"\bcurator's (answer|decision|ruling|choice)\b",
    r"\bis a decision of the curator\b",
    r"\b(his|her) (answer|decision|word|go|review|choice)\b",
